16. Frozen evaluation: all initial situations, two execution modes¶

Evaluate each learned table from all 300 starts at epsilon=0 and .1, with no updates. A random reference uses ten independent RNG replicas. The shortest-path reference has the full model and is an upper bound, not a third learning algorithm. All policies share the same starts and step cap. Means include unsuccessful capped episodes.

optimal_delivery requires success and exactly the BFS minimum action count. excess_steps is steps minus the per-start minimum and includes capped failures.

In [17]:
learned_group = {"Q-learning": q_runs, "SARSA": sarsa_runs, "Q + mask": masked_runs}
frozen_copies = [r.q.copy() for runs in learned_group.values() for r in runs]
evaluation = evaluate_group(learned_group)
assert all(np.array_equal(old,run.q) for old,run in
           zip(frozen_copies,[r for runs in learned_group.values() for r in runs]))
eval_summary = evaluation_summary(evaluation)
learned_evaluation = evaluation[evaluation.agent.isin(learned_group)]
save_figure(plot_evaluation(learned_evaluation), "09_frozen_learned_policy_evaluation")
display(eval_summary[["agent","mode","seed_replicates","return","return_se","success",
                      "steps","illegal_actions","wall_hits","optimal_delivery","truncated"]].round(3))

# Plot references separately so the random agent does not obscure learned-policy details.
compared = pd.concat([eval_summary[eval_summary["mode"] == "Greedy"],
                      eval_summary[eval_summary["mode"] == "Reference"]], ignore_index=True)

    ax.set_yticks(y,compared.agent); ax.invert_yaxis()

Inspect an unsuccessful frozen policy, if one occurs¶

Successful exploratory training does not guarantee that every finite learned table produces a successful greedy policy. We inspect the first capped greedy SARSA trip in sorted seed/start order, reproduce its exact evaluation random stream, and show its final decisions and action values. Repeated wall actions or state cycles explain how this particular frozen policy fails. Constant-step-size noise and limited experience are possible contributors; this inspection alone does not establish their causal effects.

In [18]:
failed_sarsa=evaluation[(evaluation.agent=="SARSA") & (evaluation["mode"]=="Greedy") & evaluation.truncated]
SARSA_CAPPED_TRIPS=len(failed_sarsa)
if not failed_sarsa.empty:
    failure=failed_sarsa.sort_values(["train_seed","start_state"]).iloc[0]
    failure_seed=int(failure.train_seed)
    failure_start=int(failure.start_state)
    failure_run=next(r for r in sarsa_runs if r.config.seed==failure_seed)
    start_index=int(np.flatnonzero(EVAL_STARTS==failure_start)[0])
    child_seed=np.random.SeedSequence(100_000+failure_seed).spawn(len(EVAL_STARTS))[start_index]
    failure_route=rollout(TaxiEnv(),failure_run.q,failure_start,epsilon=0,max_steps=MAX_STEPS,seed=child_seed)
    assert not failure_route["success"] and failure_route["steps"]==int(failure.steps)
    assert failure_route["return"]==failure["return"]
    trace=pd.DataFrame([{ "step":i+1,"state":s,"position_and_service_state":env.decode(s),
                          "action":env.action_names[a],"reward":reward,"next_state":ns}
                        for i,(s,a,reward,ns) in enumerate(zip(failure_route["states"][:-1],failure_route["actions"],
                                                                  failure_route["rewards"],failure_route["states"][1:]))])
    print(f"Reproduced capped greedy SARSA trip: seed={failure_seed}, start={failure_start}. "
          f"There were {SARSA_CAPPED_TRIPS} capped trips out of {len(SEEDS)*len(EVAL_STARTS)} greedy SARSA evaluations.")
    display(trace.tail(10))
    inspected_state=failure_route["states"][-2]
    values=failure_run.q[inspected_state]
    display(pd.DataFrame({"action":env.action_names,"estimated_Q":values,
                          "greedy_maximizer":values==values.max(),
                          "next_state":[env.transition(inspected_state,a)[0] for a in range(6)],
                          "immediate_reward":[env.transition(inspected_state,a)[1] for a in range(6)]}))
    trace.to_csv(TABLES/"reproduced_sarsa_failure_trace.csv",index=False)
else:
    print("No capped greedy SARSA trips in this run.")

17. Compare parameter settings under common greedy execution¶

Training return combines learning quality with the immediate cost of exploration. The next table evaluates every alpha, gamma, and epsilon setting with epsilon=0 over all 300 starts. This prevents a low-exploration setting from looking better solely because it performs fewer random actions during training.

In [19]:

18. Convergence behavior at saved checkpoints¶

Evaluate Q-learning snapshots over all 300 starts and compare their Q-values with the model solution at the same gamma=.95. Q error includes only the 400 valid decision states and their six actions. SARSA's exploratory target differs, so it is not scored against Q* as though it estimated the same quantity.

Delivery success, optimal route frequency, and complete Q-table accuracy are distinct. Good performance from common starts can precede accurate rarely visited action values.

A policy map must specify passenger and destination context. The two maps hold the destination at B and compare a passenger waiting at R with a passenger on board. Labels P/D indicate pickup/drop-off actions; arrows show one maximizing movement action. Ties in actual rollouts remain random.

20. Where is the learned policy efficient?¶

These matrices average the fraction of minimum-length deliveries across all 25 taxi positions and ten trained seeds for each pickup/destination pair. Diagonal pairs never occur as initial states. They expose performance across the task, beyond the demo route.

22. Measured findings and interpretation¶

This discussion is calculated from the actual tables. Rankings are descriptive within the tested budget and seed list. Small differences relative to seed uncertainty do not establish a universal best parameter or a statistically significant advantage.

  • Correctness: all 13 implementation check groups and 5 complete-study checks passed. Every one of the 3,000 Taxi transitions and 500 masks matched the installed Gymnasium reference.

  • Learning speed: Q-learning mean return moved from -97.64 in the first 500 episodes to 2.26 in the last 500. In the alpha study, alpha=0.7 had the highest first-500 return (-59.17); inspect late behavior separately.

  • Exact benchmark: over all 300 equally weighted initial states, the minimum route averages 13.07 actions and the optimal undiscounted return is 7.93. The optimum is start-dependent, not one fixed trip length.

  • Final Q-learning policy: greedy success was 100.00%, mean return 7.900 (SE 0.017), mean steps 13.100, and minimum-length delivery frequency 98.50%. Truncation was 0.00%; failures remain included.

  • Exploration cost: frozen Q-learning at epsilon=.1 returned 2.14 with 0.453 illegal service attempts and 0.266 wall no-ops per trip. Greedy return was 7.90; these are different execution policies even though Q is unchanged.

  • SARSA comparison: greedy return -22.26, success 85.60%; exploratory return -8.54 with 0.704 illegal attempts. There were 432 capped greedy trips out of 3000 evaluations. The failure inspection reproduces one such trip if present; exploratory actions can escape a frozen greedy loop. Its sampled next-action target and finite noisy estimates differ from Q-learning's greedy target. Use these measurements rather than assuming a universal ranking.

  • Masking extension: unmasked Q-learning made 0.444 illegal attempts per late training episode; masked training made zero by construction. Masked greedy success was 100.00% and optimal-route frequency 99.33%; masked exploratory return was 6.12. The extra validity rules are supplied knowledge.

  • Exploration schedule: fixed .3 gave late return -14.51 and 1.766 illegal attempts; decay gave 7.46 and 0.036. Lower late exploration and the learned policy both affect this comparison.

  • Q-value accuracy: final mean absolute Q error over 400 valid decision states ×6 actions was 2.8503; mean greedy optimal-route frequency was 98.50%. Successful routes and complete-table accuracy are distinct measurements.

  • alpha under common greedy evaluation: alpha=0.1 had the highest observed mean return (7.930); SEs across trained seed means are in the endpoint table. Success ranged 100.0%–100.0%; optimal-route frequency ranged 96.4%–100.0%. This separates learned policy quality from training exploration costs.

  • gamma under common greedy evaluation: gamma=1 had the highest observed mean return (7.908); SEs across trained seed means are in the endpoint table. Success ranged 95.4%–100.0%; optimal-route frequency ranged 95.3%–98.9%. This separates learned policy quality from training exploration costs.

  • epsilon under common greedy evaluation: epsilon=0.3 had the highest observed mean return (7.922); SEs across trained seed means are in the endpoint table. Success ranged 100.0%–100.0%; optimal-route frequency ranged 98.5%–99.6%. This separates learned policy quality from training exploration costs.

23. What the results establish, and what remains limited¶

Off-policy implication: the Q-learning backup uses a greedy future action, while its training behavior may still pick an illegal or inefficient random action. Frozen greedy versus exploratory evaluation directly measures this distinction. A learned Q-table can therefore support efficient exploitation while continued exploration remains costly.

Rule compliance: Taxi's illegal actions are abstract service-rule violations. The simulator does not model speed, pedestrians, road collisions, or physical driving safety. Masking excludes some operations by supplied rules, while still allowing legal inefficient decisions. Zero masked violations are expected by construction, not a discovered safety theorem.

Convergence: finite curves and Q-error measurements show empirical progress or stabilization. Constant alpha, a finite budget, and a positive epsilon floor alone do not establish theoretical convergence conditions. See Watkins and Dayan (1992).

Evidence limits: only ten training seeds and a small set of parameter values are tested. One-factor studies miss interactions. Deterministic movement and fixed destinations simplify the task. The 200-action cap censors long failures; truncation is reported. The planning reference has knowledge the learner lacks. All-start evaluation covers the initial-state distribution, but a single exploratory trip per start and trained seed still has sampling noise.

Future experiments: noisy movement, changing destinations, different maps, more training, Expected SARSA, or a separate test set of changed environments. These are extensions; the current experiment does not establish generalization to them.

25. Viva preparation¶

1. What is a Taxi state, and why is taxi position alone insufficient? A state includes taxi row/column, passenger location or onboard status, and destination. The same taxi position requires different actions depending on whom it is serving and where they must go.

2. Why are there 500 encodings, 400 decision states, and 300 initial states? The storage count is 25 × 5 × 4. Valid nonterminal states include 300 waiting-passenger cases and 100 onboard cases. Initial states exclude onboard passengers and passenger-equals-destination cases. Four successful terminal observations are additionally reachable.

3. Why is the state Markov? In the dry, fixed-destination task, the encoded state and chosen action determine the next-state and reward distribution without needing earlier history. Rainy/fickle variants are outside this project's scope.

4. What are the rewards and an easily misunderstood dropoff rule? Ordinary actions give −1, illegal service attempts −10, and successful delivery +20. Dropping an onboard passenger at a wrong landmark is legal −1 and nonterminal; it is tracked separately.

5. What does the Q-learning update do? It moves Q(s,a) toward the observed reward plus gamma times the best estimated next-action value. Alpha controls the size of this correction; it learns from transitions without requiring the BFS answer.

6. How do terminal and cutoff updates differ? Successful delivery still updates with target +20 and zero continuation. An administrative time cutoff still updates the last nonterminal transition with its bootstrapped continuation value.

7. What do gamma and epsilon control? Gamma weights future rewards in learning. Epsilon selects random exploration. We use a common undiscounted evaluation metric when comparing gamma settings and retain the chosen evaluation epsilon explicitly.

8. Why randomly break maximizing ties? Initial Q-values are equal. Always taking the first maximum would add an arbitrary action-order preference. Uniform tie-breaking treats equally valued actions symmetrically.

9. Why evaluate all 300 initial states and multiple training seeds? Uniform state coverage checks every allowed starting situation. Independent trained seeds show learning variability. These are different sources of evidence; 300 evaluations of one table are not 300 trained agents.

10. How is the optimal reference calculated? BFS supplies wall-respecting distances. Optimal steps equal taxi-to-passenger distance, pickup, passenger-to-destination distance, and dropoff; optimal undiscounted return is 21 minus those steps.

11. Is action masking learned safety? It is supplied action-validity knowledge restricting selection and backups. It can enforce some operational rules, but it is neither independent discovery of those rules nor evidence of physical driving safety.

12. Does a stable curve or gamma=1 prove convergence? No. The run is finite with constant alpha. Gamma=1 requires appropriate episodic/properness assumptions; bad policies may loop. We report empirical performance, truncation, and the conditions tested.

The Taxi task originates in Dietterich's formulation. The project applies tabular TD control and experimental analysis to this task; it does not claim to introduce a new RL algorithm.
